title: Sets, relations and functions
subject: Mathematics
summary: A set is a collection of distinct objects, a relation links elements of two sets, and a function assigns exactly one output to each input.
points: Set operations include union, intersection, difference and complement.
A relation from A to B is a subset of A × B.
A function f: A → B is one-one if different inputs give different outputs, and onto if every element of B is an output.

formulas.name: Union size
formulas.expr: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

formulas.name: Three sets
formulas.expr: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = Σn(A) − Σn(A ∩ B) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C)

mistakes: Calling a relation a function when one input has two outputs.

title: Trigonometric functions
subject: Mathematics
summary: Trigonometric functions extend the right-triangle ratios to all angles using the unit circle, with periodicity and identities.
points: Sine and cosine have period 2π; tangent has period π.
Signs change by quadrant: ASTC (all, sine, tangent, cosine positive).
Key identities include sin²x + cos²x = 1 and sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x.

formulas.name: Double angle
formulas.expr: sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, cos 2x = 1 − 2sin²x

formulas.name: General solution
formulas.expr: sin θ = sin α ⇒ θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿα

example: sin 150° = sin 30° = 1/2, because 150° is in the second quadrant where sine is positive.
mistakes: Forgetting the ± when solving trigonometric equations.

title: Complex numbers
subject: Mathematics
summary: A complex number has the form a + bi, where i² = −1, and it can be represented as a point in the complex plane.
points: The modulus |a + bi| = √(a² + b²) and the argument gives its direction.
Multiplication adds arguments and multiplies moduli.
The conjugate of a + bi is a − bi, and z × z̄ = |z|².

formulas.name: Polar form
formulas.expr: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ)

formulas.name: De Moivre
formulas.expr: (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ

mistakes: Simplifying i² as 1 instead of −1.

title: Permutations and combinations
subject: Mathematics
summary: Permutations count arrangements where order matters; combinations count selections where it does not.
points: nPr = n!/(n − r)! and nCr = n!/[r!(n − r)!].
nCr = nC(n − r), and nC0 = nCn = 1.
The fundamental principle of counting multiplies independent choices.
example: Choosing 3 students from 10 is 10C3 = 120; arranging them in a row is 10P3 = 720.
mistakes: Using permutations when only a group is being chosen.

title: Binomial theorem
subject: Mathematics
summary: The binomial theorem expands (x + y)ⁿ as a sum of terms with binomial coefficients.
points: The general term is Tᵣ₊₁ = nCr xⁿ⁻ʳ yʳ.
There are n + 1 terms in the expansion.
Binomial coefficients are symmetric and sum to 2ⁿ.
mistakes: Starting the term index at 1 instead of 0.

title: Sequences and series
subject: Mathematics
summary: A sequence is an ordered list, and a series is its sum; arithmetic and geometric sequences have closed formulas.
points: AP: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d and Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n − 1)d].
GP: aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹ and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.
An infinite GP converges only when |r| < 1.
mistakes: Using the infinite sum formula when |r| ≥ 1.

title: Straight lines
subject: Mathematics
summary: A straight line in the plane is described by its slope and a point, or by a linear equation in x and y.
points: Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
Forms include slope-intercept y = mx + c and point-slope y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.

formulas.name: Distance from a point to a line

example: A line through (1, 2) with slope 3 is y − 2 = 3(x − 1), or y = 3x − 1.
mistakes: Saying perpendicular lines have equal slopes; their product is −1.

title: Conic sections
subject: Mathematics
summary: A conic section is the curve formed by cutting a cone, giving circles, ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas.
points: A circle has eccentricity 0 and an ellipse less than 1.
A parabola has eccentricity 1; a hyperbola has eccentricity greater than 1.
Each conic has a standard equation with a focus and directrix.
example: y² = 12x is a parabola with 4a = 12, so a = 3 and the focus is (3, 0).
mistakes: Mixing the ellipse and hyperbola equations; the hyperbola has a minus sign.

title: Limits and derivatives
subject: Mathematics
summary: A limit describes the value a function approaches, and the derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change.
points: The derivative is defined as the limit of the difference quotient.
Standard derivatives include d(xⁿ)/dx = nxⁿ⁻¹, d(sin x)/dx = cos x and d(eˣ)/dx = eˣ.
Rules include product, quotient and chain rules.

formulas.name: Trig derivatives
formulas.expr: d(sin x)/dx = cos x, d(cos x)/dx = −sin x

mistakes: Forgetting the inner derivative in the chain rule.

title: Matrices and determinants
subject: Mathematics
summary: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, and its determinant is a value that helps solve systems and find inverses.
points: Matrix multiplication is possible when columns of the first equal rows of the second.
AB is usually not equal to BA.
A square matrix has an inverse only if its determinant is non-zero.
example: For A = [[2, 1], [3, 4]], |A| = 8 − 3 = 5, so A is invertible.
mistakes: Assuming matrix multiplication is commutative.

title: Integration
subject: Mathematics
summary: Integration reverses differentiation and measures accumulated change, including areas under curves.
points: Indefinite integrals include a constant of integration C.
The fundamental theorem links definite integrals to antiderivatives.
Methods include substitution, by parts and partial fractions.
example: ∫₀² 3x² dx = [x³]₀² = 8.
mistakes: Omitting + C in an indefinite integral.
Forgetting to change limits when substituting in a definite integral.

title: Differential equations
subject: Mathematics
summary: A differential equation relates a function to its derivatives, and solving it means finding the function.
points: Order is the highest derivative present; degree is its power after clearing radicals.
Variable separable equations are solved by separating and integrating.
Linear equations of first order use an integrating factor.
example: dy/dx = 2x gives y = x² + C.
mistakes: Calling the power of the highest derivative the order; that is the degree.

title: Vectors and three-dimensional geometry
subject: Mathematics
summary: Vectors have magnitude and direction, and three-dimensional geometry uses coordinates and vectors to describe lines and planes.
points: The dot product measures alignment: a·b = |a||b| cos θ.
The cross product gives a perpendicular vector and measures area.
A line in space is described by a point and a direction vector.
example: If a·b = 0, the vectors are perpendicular.
mistakes: Using the dot product when a perpendicular vector is needed.

title: Probability and Bayes' theorem
subject: Mathematics
summary: Probability for multiple events uses conditional probability, independence and Bayes' theorem.
points: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) for P(B) > 0.
Independent events satisfy P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).
Bayes' theorem updates a probability using new evidence.
example: If a test is 90% accurate and a disease is rare, a positive result may still have a modest probability of disease.
mistakes: Assuming rare events become likely after one positive test.

title: Units, dimensions and errors
subject: Physics
summary: Physical quantities are measured in SI units, and dimensional analysis checks equations and converts units.
points: The seven SI base units include metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.
Dimensions express a quantity in terms of M, L, T, A, K, mol and cd.
Errors combine differently for sums and products.
example: Force has dimensions [M L T⁻²], the same as mass × acceleration.
mistakes: Adding absolute errors when multiplying quantities instead of adding relative errors.

title: Vectors and projectile motion
subject: Physics
summary: Projectile motion combines constant horizontal velocity with vertical acceleration due to gravity.
points: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent.
Maximum height is reached when vertical velocity is zero.
Range is greatest at 45° for a given speed on level ground.
example: A ball thrown at 20 m/s at 30° has range 400 × sin 60° / 9.8 ≈ 35.3 m.
mistakes: Using the total speed in the vertical equation instead of its vertical component.

title: Rotational motion
subject: Physics
summary: Rotational motion describes bodies spinning about an axis, using torque, moment of inertia and angular momentum.
points: Torque = r × F and changes angular momentum.
Moment of inertia depends on mass distribution about the axis.
Angular momentum is conserved when external torque is zero.
example: A skater pulling in their arms reduces I, so ω increases to conserve L.
aliases: system of particles and rotational motion
mistakes: Treating moment of inertia as a fixed property; it depends on the chosen axis.

title: Thermodynamics
subject: Physics
summary: Thermodynamics studies heat, work and internal energy, governed by the laws of thermodynamics.
points: First law: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW (energy conservation).
Second law: entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
Isothermal, adiabatic, isochoric and isobaric processes each hold one quantity constant.
example: In an adiabatic process no heat is exchanged, so ΔQ = 0 and ΔU = −ΔW.
mistakes: Using Celsius temperatures in efficiency formulas; kelvin is required.

title: Oscillations and waves
subject: Physics
summary: Oscillations repeat in time, and waves carry energy through space with a frequency, wavelength and speed.
points: Simple harmonic motion has acceleration proportional to displacement and directed towards equilibrium.
The period of a simple pendulum is independent of mass.
Waves can be transverse or longitudinal and show superposition.
example: A 1 m pendulum on Earth has T ≈ 2π√(1/9.8) ≈ 2.0 s.
mistakes: Thinking the pendulum period depends on the bob's mass.

title: Electric charges and fields
subject: Physics
summary: Stationary charges create electric fields and potentials, described by Coulomb's law and Gauss's law.
points: Like charges repel and opposite charges attract.
The electric field points away from positive charge and towards negative charge.
Electric potential is work done per unit charge.
example: Doubling the distance between two charges reduces the force to one quarter.
mistakes: Using degrees instead of metres in Coulomb's law, or mixing microcoulombs with coulombs.

title: Current electricity and circuits
subject: Physics
summary: Current electricity studies charge flow in conductors, including resistance, emf and circuit laws.
points: Drift velocity is the average velocity of electrons in a conductor.
Kirchhoff's junction rule conserves charge and the loop rule conserves energy.
Terminal voltage is less than emf when current flows because of internal resistance.

formulas.name: Drift relation
formulas.symbols: n density, A area, v_d drift velocity

example: A cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω driving 2 A gives terminal voltage 4 V.
mistakes: Ignoring internal resistance when calculating terminal voltage.

title: Magnetism and electromagnetic induction
subject: Physics
summary: Moving charges and currents create magnetic fields, and changing magnetic flux induces an emf.
points: A charged particle moving in a magnetic field experiences a force perpendicular to its velocity.
Faraday's law gives the induced emf as the rate of change of flux.
Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change causing it.

formulas.name: Magnetic force
formulas.expr: F = q v B sin θ

formulas.name: Force on a wire
formulas.expr: F = B I l sin θ

example: Doubling the rate at which a magnet moves into a coil doubles the induced emf.
mistakes: Thinking a steady magnetic field through a stationary coil induces an emf.

title: Ray and wave optics
subject: Physics
summary: Ray optics treats light as straight lines through mirrors and lenses; wave optics explains interference, diffraction and polarisation.
points: Refraction follows Snell's law and total internal reflection occurs beyond the critical angle.
Young's double slit produces alternating bright and dark fringes.
The lens and mirror formulas use a sign convention.

formulas.name: Snell's law
formulas.expr: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r

formulas.name: Fringe width
formulas.symbols: D slit-screen distance, d slit separation

example: Light going from water (n = 1.33) to air has sin C = 1/1.33, so C ≈ 49°.
mistakes: Using the lens formula without consistent sign conventions.

title: Dual nature, atoms and nuclei
subject: Physics
summary: Light and matter show both wave and particle behaviour, and nuclear physics explains atomic structure, radioactivity and energy release.
points: The photoelectric effect shows light behaving as photons.
de Broglie wavelength links momentum and wavelength.
Radioactive decay is random and follows an exponential law.
example: After one half-life, half of a radioactive sample remains.
aliases: dual nature of radiation and matter
mistakes: Thinking intensity changes the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons; frequency does.

title: Semiconductor electronics
subject: Physics
summary: Semiconductors have conductivity between conductors and insulators, and doping lets them form diodes and transistors.
points: n-type semiconductors have extra electrons; p-type have holes.
A p–n junction diode conducts in forward bias and blocks in reverse bias.
A transistor can amplify or switch signals.
example: A diode used as a rectifier converts alternating current into pulsating direct current.
mistakes: Thinking a diode conducts equally in both directions.

title: Atomic structure
subject: Chemistry
summary: Atoms have a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons in orbitals described by quantum numbers.
points: The four quantum numbers are principal, azimuthal, magnetic and spin.
Orbitals fill by the Aufbau principle, Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle.
Electronic configuration explains periodic properties.
example: Sodium (Z = 11) has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.
mistakes: Filling 3d before 4s; 4s fills first.

title: Chemical and ionic equilibrium
subject: Chemistry
summary: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium when forward and reverse rates are equal, and ionic equilibrium covers acids, bases and solubility.
points: At equilibrium concentrations stay constant, though reactions continue.
Le Chatelier's principle predicts the shift when conditions change.
The ionic product of water K_w = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
example: Adding more reactant shifts the equilibrium towards products.
mistakes: Thinking equilibrium means equal concentrations of reactants and products.

title: Chemical thermodynamics
subject: Chemistry
summary: Chemical thermodynamics predicts whether a reaction releases energy and whether it can happen spontaneously.
points: Enthalpy change ΔH measures heat at constant pressure.
Entropy change ΔS measures dispersal of energy.
A reaction is spontaneous when ΔG is negative.
example: Combustion has negative ΔH and is spontaneous, even though it needs activation energy to start.
mistakes: Saying a spontaneous reaction happens instantly; it may be very slow.

title: Electrochemistry
subject: Chemistry
summary: Electrochemistry studies the relationship between chemical reactions and electrical energy in cells and electrolysis.
points: Oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode.
Standard electrode potentials predict cell voltage.
The Nernst equation adjusts cell potential for concentration.
example: A cell with E°cell > 0 can drive a spontaneous reaction.
mistakes: Swapping anode and cathode definitions between galvanic cells and electrolysis.

title: Chemical kinetics
subject: Chemistry
summary: Chemical kinetics studies reaction rates and the factors that change them.
points: Rate depends on concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts.
Order is determined experimentally, not from the balanced equation.
Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for reaction.
example: A first-order reaction with k = 0.0693 s⁻¹ has a half-life of about 10 s.
mistakes: Reading reaction order from coefficients in the balanced equation.

title: Coordination compounds
subject: Chemistry
summary: Coordination compounds contain a central metal ion bonded to ligands, and their structure explains colour and magnetism.
points: The coordination number is the number of ligand donor atoms bonded to the metal.
Ligands are classified by denticity (monodentate, bidentate, polydentate).
Crystal field theory explains splitting of d orbitals and colour.

formulas.name: Oxidation state
formulas.expr: charge on complex = x + Σ ligand charges

formulas.name: EAN rule
formulas.expr: effective atomic number = Z − oxidation state + 2 × coordination number

example: In [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ the coordination number is 4 and copper's oxidation state is +2.
mistakes: Counting ligands instead of donor atoms for polydentate ligands.

title: Organic reaction mechanisms
subject: Chemistry
summary: Organic reactions proceed through mechanisms such as substitution, addition and elimination, driven by electron movement.
points: Nucleophiles donate electron pairs; electrophiles accept them.
SN1 proceeds via a carbocation and SN2 in one step with inversion.
Markovnikov's rule predicts addition to unsymmetrical alkenes.

formulas.name: Markovnikov addition
formulas.expr: H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens

example: HBr added to propene gives 2-bromopropane as the major product.
mistakes: Drawing a carbocation where a carbanion belongs, or ignoring rearrangements.

title: Biomolecules and polymers
subject: Chemistry
summary: Biomolecules such as carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids carry out life processes, and polymers are large molecules built from repeating units.
points: Monosaccharides are simple sugars; polysaccharides are polymers of sugars.
Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
Addition polymers form from alkenes; condensation polymers release a small molecule.

formulas.name: Degree of polymerisation
formulas.expr: DP = molar mass of polymer / molar mass of monomer

example: Nylon is a condensation polymer; polythene is an addition polymer.
mistakes: Confusing addition and condensation polymerisation.

title: Cell cycle and cell division
subject: Biology
summary: The cell cycle is the sequence of growth, DNA replication and division that produces new cells.
points: Interphase includes G1, S (DNA replication) and G2.
Mitosis produces two identical diploid cells for growth and repair.
Meiosis produces four haploid cells and creates genetic variation.
example: Crossing over in prophase I of meiosis mixes maternal and paternal genes.
mistakes: Saying meiosis produces identical cells; it produces genetically varied gametes.

title: Plant physiology
subject: Biology
summary: Plant physiology explains how plants absorb water, make food, transport materials and respond to their environment.
points: Water moves up xylem mainly by transpiration pull.
Photosynthesis has light reactions and the Calvin cycle.
Plant hormones such as auxin control growth and tropisms.
example: Stomata close in dry conditions to reduce water loss, which also limits carbon dioxide intake.
mistakes: Thinking photosynthesis happens only in daylight and respiration only at night; respiration is continuous.

title: Human reproduction and reproductive health
subject: Biology
summary: Human reproduction involves gamete production, fertilisation, implantation and development of the embryo.
points: The menstrual cycle is about 28 days, with ovulation near the middle.
Fertilisation normally happens in the fallopian tube.
Reproductive health includes contraception, prenatal care and prevention of infections.
example: The corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which maintains the uterine lining.
mistakes: Saying the embryo implants immediately after fertilisation; it travels to the uterus first.

title: Molecular basis of inheritance
subject: Biology
summary: DNA stores genetic information and is copied, transcribed into RNA and translated into proteins.
points: DNA is a double helix with complementary base pairing: A–T and G–C.
Transcription makes mRNA from a DNA template; translation builds a protein at the ribosome.
Mutations change the DNA sequence and may alter the protein.
example: A codon of three mRNA bases specifies one amino acid.
mistakes: Thinking RNA contains thymine; it contains uracil instead.

title: Biotechnology
subject: Biology
summary: Biotechnology uses living organisms or their parts to make useful products, often through genetic engineering.
points: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences and ligase joins fragments.
Plasmids carry foreign genes into bacteria.
Applications include insulin, vaccines and genetically modified crops.
example: Human insulin is produced by bacteria carrying the human insulin gene.
mistakes: Confusing restriction enzymes (cut) with ligase (join).

title: Organisms, populations and ecosystems
subject: Biology
summary: Ecology studies how organisms interact with each other and their environment at population and ecosystem levels.
points: Population growth can be exponential or limited by carrying capacity.
Interactions include competition, predation, parasitism and mutualism.
Productivity and decomposition drive ecosystem function.
example: A population at carrying capacity grows slowly because births and deaths balance.
mistakes: Assuming populations always grow exponentially; resources limit growth.

title: Human health and disease
subject: Biology
summary: Health depends on physical, mental and social well-being, and disease can be infectious or non-infectious.
points: Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites.
Immunity can be innate or acquired, and active immunity follows infection or vaccination.
Lifestyle diseases such as diabetes have genetic and environmental causes.
example: Vaccination exposes the body to an antigen so it produces memory cells without causing the disease.
mistakes: Thinking antibiotics treat viral infections.

title: Accounting equation and journal entries
subject: Accountancy
summary: Accounting records transactions using double entry, and the accounting equation keeps assets equal to liabilities plus capital.
points: Every transaction affects at least two accounts, with equal debits and credits.
Assets = Liabilities + Capital must always balance.
Journal entries record the accounts, amounts and narration.
example: Buying furniture for cash increases furniture and decreases cash, so total assets do not change.
mistakes: Debiting an increase in capital; capital increases are credited.

title: Ledger and trial balance
subject: Accountancy
summary: The ledger collects transactions by account, and the trial balance checks that total debits equal total credits.
points: Posting transfers journal entries to ledger accounts.
A trial balance lists debit and credit balances; equality does not prove there are no errors.
Errors of principle and complete omission are not revealed by a trial balance.
example: A purchase of goods on credit is debited to Purchases and credited to the supplier's account.
mistakes: Assuming a balanced trial balance means the accounts are error-free.

title: Depreciation
subject: Accountancy
summary: Depreciation allocates the cost of a fixed asset over its useful life.
points: Straight-line method charges an equal amount each year.
Written-down value method charges a fixed percentage of the reducing balance.
Depreciation is a non-cash expense that reduces profit.
example: A machine costing ₹1,00,000 with ₹10,000 scrap over 9 years depreciates ₹10,000 a year on the straight-line method.
mistakes: Charging depreciation on the scrap value instead of the depreciable cost.

title: Financial statements
subject: Accountancy
summary: Financial statements report profit or loss and the financial position of a business.
points: The trading account finds gross profit; the profit and loss account finds net profit.
The balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and capital on a date.
Ratios such as current ratio and gross profit ratio analyse performance.
example: Sales ₹5,00,000 and cost of goods sold ₹3,00,000 give gross profit ₹2,00,000.
mistakes: Treating capital as an expense in the profit and loss account.

title: Principles of management
subject: Business Studies
summary: Management is getting work done through people by planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling.
points: Fayol proposed fourteen principles including division of work and unity of command.
Taylor emphasised scientific management and standardisation.
Coordination is the essence of management.
example: Unity of command means an employee should receive orders from one superior at a time.
mistakes: Confusing unity of command with unity of direction.

title: Marketing management
subject: Business Studies
summary: Marketing identifies customer needs and creates, communicates and delivers value to satisfy them profitably.
points: The marketing mix has product, price, place and promotion.
Branding, labelling and packaging influence buying decisions.
The product life cycle has introduction, growth, maturity and decline stages.
example: A new phone is priced high at launch (skimming) and lowered as competitors arrive.
mistakes: Treating marketing as only advertising; the product, price and distribution matter too.

title: Demand, supply and market equilibrium
subject: Economics
summary: Demand and supply curves determine price and quantity in a market, and elasticity measures responsiveness.
points: Demand falls as price rises, other things equal (law of demand).
Equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Elasticity measures the percentage change in quantity for a percentage change in price.

formulas.name: Price elasticity of demand
formulas.expr: E_d = (% change in quantity) / (% change in price)

example: If a 10% price rise reduces quantity by 20%, demand is elastic (|E| = 2).
mistakes: Confusing a movement along the curve with a shift of the curve.

title: National income
subject: Economics
summary: National income measures the value of goods and services produced in an economy over a period.
points: GDP is the value of final goods and services produced within a country.
GNP adds net factor income from abroad.
The expenditure method sums consumption, investment, government spending and net exports.

formulas.name: GNP
formulas.expr: GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad

example: GDP counts production inside the country regardless of who owns the factory.
mistakes: Counting intermediate goods, which double-counts output.

title: Market structures
subject: Economics
summary: Market structure describes competition among firms, from perfect competition to monopoly.
points: Perfect competition has many sellers, identical products and free entry.
A monopoly has one seller and barriers to entry.
Monopolistic competition has many sellers with differentiated products.
example: A farmer selling wheat is closer to perfect competition; a local electricity supplier is closer to a monopoly.
mistakes: Assuming a monopolist charges any price; demand still limits sales.

title: Data structures and algorithms
subject: Computer Science
summary: Data structures organise data so operations are efficient, and algorithm analysis compares their cost as input grows.
points: Arrays give fast index access; linked lists give fast insertion and deletion.
Stacks are last-in-first-out; queues are first-in-first-out.
Big O describes the growth of running time with input size.
example: A stack is used for undo history; the most recent action is undone first.
mistakes: Using a list where repeated search makes a hash table or set much faster.

title: Databases and SQL
subject: Computer Science
summary: A relational database stores data in tables linked by keys and is queried with SQL.
points: A primary key uniquely identifies a row; a foreign key references another table.
SELECT retrieves data with WHERE, ORDER BY and JOIN.
Normalisation reduces redundancy and update anomalies.

formulas.name: Basic query
formulas.expr: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

formulas.name: Join
formulas.expr: SELECT * FROM A JOIN B ON A.id = B.a_id;

example: A school database may have a students table and a marks table linked by student id.
mistakes: Forgetting the WHERE clause on an UPDATE or DELETE, which affects every row.

title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning
subject: Computer Science
summary: AI builds systems that perform tasks needing intelligence, and machine learning learns patterns from data instead of explicit rules.
points: Supervised learning uses labelled examples; unsupervised learning finds structure; reinforcement learning learns from reward.
Overfitting means fitting training data too closely and generalising poorly.
Bias in data produces biased predictions.
example: A spam filter trained on labelled emails is a supervised classification model.
mistakes: Judging a model only on training accuracy; it may not generalise.

title: Literary devices and analysis
subject: English
summary: Literary devices are techniques writers use to create meaning and effect, and analysis explains how they work in context.
points: Simile compares using like or as; metaphor states one thing is another.
Personification gives human qualities to non-human things.
Irony, symbolism and imagery shape tone and theme.
example: The wind whispered through the trees personifies the wind and creates a quiet mood.
mistakes: Naming a device without explaining its effect on meaning or tone.

title: Formal writing: letters, reports and articles
subject: English
summary: Formal writing follows a clear structure and a polite, impersonal register suited to its purpose and audience.
points: A formal letter includes sender details, date, receiver, subject, salutation, body and closing.
A report states the purpose, findings and conclusion.
An article has a headline, an engaging opening, developed paragraphs and a closing.
example: A complaint letter states the problem, gives evidence and asks for a specific remedy.
mistakes: Using contractions and slang in a formal letter.
